title: Modes & stream ciphers
syllabusUnit: Unit II: Block Cipher Modes & RC4 Stream Cipher
covers: ECB/CBC/CTR/GCM, RC4, pseudo-random numbers, key distribution
learningGoals: You will be able to explain why Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode leaks data patterns.
You will be able to diagram Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) with an Initialization Vector (IV).
You will be able to contrast CTR mode and GCM authenticated encryption.

lessonCards.title: The ECB Penguin Problem
lessonCards.analogy: Coloring every white pixel red and every black pixel blue leaves the penguin silhouette perfectly visible.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Electronic Codebook (ECB) encrypts each 128-bit block independently. Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking visual patterns.
lessonCards.example: Encrypting a bitmap photo in ECB preserves the clear outline of the image.

lessonCards.title: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) & IV
lessonCards.analogy: Locking each box with a chain link hooked to the previous box's locked padlock.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Cipher Block Chaining XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption. The first block uses a random Initialization Vector (IV).
lessonCards.example: Even if all plaintext blocks are identical, CBC outputs totally random-looking ciphertext.

lessonCards.title: CTR Mode & GCM Authenticated Encryption
lessonCards.analogy: Turning a block cipher into a super-fast stream cipher by encrypting a ticking counter.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Counter (CTR) mode encrypts Nonce + Counter to create a keystream, enabling parallel processing. Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) adds an authentication tag (AEAD).
lessonCards.example: TLS 1.3 requires AEAD modes like AES-GCM to prevent padding oracle tampering.

questions.prompt: Why is Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode considered unsafe for encrypting files larger than one block?
options: Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, exposing data patterns
questions.explanation: Because identical input blocks always map to identical output blocks, images and repeating records remain clearly discernible.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The famous ECB Linux Penguin demo shows visual patterns remain visible.
Keys do not expire based on block mode.
ECB works on any block cipher width.
Headers are encrypted, not deleted.
questions.realWorldExample: In 2013, Adobe suffered a breach where password hints and repeated passwords were exposed due to ECB mode.

questions.prompt: In Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, what is the role of the Initialization Vector (IV)?
options: To randomize the first block so identical messages produce different ciphertexts
questions.explanation: An unpredictable, unique IV ensures that two identical plaintexts encrypted with the same key produce completely different ciphertexts.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The IV randomizes the start of the CBC chain.
Passwords must never be stored in an unencrypted IV.
IV calculation adds a slight overhead, not speed.
Block ciphers do not compress data.
questions.realWorldExample: In CBC mode, the IV is transmitted in the clear alongside the ciphertext; it needs to be unique, not secret.

questions.prompt: What major performance advantage does Counter (CTR) mode have over CBC mode?
options: Blocks can be encrypted and decrypted in parallel across multiple CPU cores
CTR mode requires no secret key
CTR mode does not use electricity
questions.explanation: Since the input to each block is simply Nonce + Counter, all blocks can be calculated simultaneously on independent processor threads.
wrongExplanations: Correct! CTR mode is fully parallelizable for massive multi-gigabit throughput.
CTR mode strictly requires a symmetric secret key.
CTR does not compress data.
All computing requires power.
questions.realWorldExample: AES-CTR is the foundation of high-speed NVMe disk encryption.

questions.prompt: What critical security feature does Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) provide that CBC and CTR alone do NOT?
questions.explanation: GCM is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) mode; it generates a GMAC tag detecting any bit tampering.
wrongExplanations: Correct! GCM proves confidentiality AND message authenticity simultaneously.
Output size is identical plus a 16-byte authentication tag.
AES-GCM is symmetric, vulnerable to Grover's algorithm if keys are small.
GCM detects tampering; it does not repair damaged files.
questions.realWorldExample: TLS 1.3 completely banned plain CBC mode, mandating AEAD modes like AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.

options: A famous byte-oriented stream cipher designed by Ron Rivest in 1987
A hashing algorithm used in Bitcoin
questions.explanation: RC4 is a variable key-size stream cipher with byte-oriented operations based on a 256-byte state permutation array S.
wrongExplanations: Correct! RC4 was widely used in SSL and WEP before statistical keystream biases retired it.
RC4 is a stream cipher, not a block cipher.
Bitcoin uses SHA-256 for hashing.
RC4 is symmetric, not a digital signature.
questions.realWorldExample: RC4 was officially prohibited in all versions of TLS by RFC 7465 due to keystream biases in initial bytes.

options: An exploit where server error messages reveal whether decrypted CBC padding is valid
A machine that predicts future lottery numbers
A hardware Trojan inserted into CPUs
A technique to bypass passwords by entering spaces
questions.explanation: When servers return different errors for invalid PKCS#7 padding vs invalid decryption, attackers decrypt ciphertext byte by byte without the key.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The POODLE attack exploited SSL 3.0 CBC padding oracle flaws.
Oracle in cryptography refers to an entity that answers queries.
Padding oracle is an algorithmic flaw, not hardware.
Padding is mathematical byte alignment.
questions.realWorldExample: The POODLE and Lucky Thirteen attacks demonstrated why AEAD must be used instead of unauthenticated CBC.

ashRecap: Never use ECB mode! Use CBC with a random IV, or modern AES-GCM so you get ironclad encryption AND tamper-proof authentication in one pass!
